UI-DLG-001.statement: Modal dialogs must trap keyboard focus within the dialog container and dismiss immediately upon pressing the Escape key.
UI-DLG-001.evidence_quote: A modal panel requires interaction before the user can proceed, and the user is returned to where they were before it appeared.
UI-DLG-001.adaptation_note: Corrected 2026-09-13 audit: real Ch.8 ("Doing Things: Actions and Commands") has no "Modal Dialogs" section; "modal dialog" appears there only in passing. The genuine, dedicated treatment is the "Modal Panel" pattern in Chapter 3, which does support the general "requires interaction, returns user afterward" concept. However, a full-text search of the entire book for "focus trap" and "Escape key" returns zero hits anywhere, including in the Chapter 3 passage — the specific focus-trapping/Escape-dismissal mechanics in this rule's statement are not book-sourced and are retained as independent, still-valid accessibility engineering practice.

UI-DLG-002.title: Explicit Two-Step Confirmation for Destructive Actions
UI-DLG-002.statement: Destructive operations (e.g. deleting knowledge bases, revoking keys) must require explicit confirmation with the resource name stated, and default focus must NOT rest on the destructive button.
UI-DLG-002.adaptation_note: Citation removed 2026-09-13 audit: no "Confirming Destructive Actions" section exists anywhere in the real TOC, and the word "destructive" does not occur anywhere in the book's text outside the rule's own citation. "Irreversible" occurs exactly once (Ch.3, Modal Panel, re: Undo-ability of a half-filled form) — a discussion unrelated to confirmation dialogs or default-focus placement. This rule is retained as an independent UX safety best practice with no supporting citation from the current 18-book corpus.

UI-GEN-001.title: Strict Prohibition of Emojis in Production Interface Elements
UI-GEN-001.statement: Emojis must not be used as interface icons, status badges, buttons, or navigation indicators in production interfaces.
UI-GEN-001.adaptation_note: Citation removed 2026-09-13 audit: real Ch.5 has no "Iconography and Visual Metaphors" section (the relevant sub-heading is simply "Icons"), and the word "emoji" does not appear anywhere in the book. The real Icons content makes a narrower point — icons should share one consistent visual weight/style and shouldn't be relied on alone without text labels — with no mention of platform emojis. This rule is retained as an independent visual-consistency best practice with no supporting citation from the current 18-book corpus.

UI-LAW-001.title: Jakob's Law: Conform to Familiar User Interface Mental Models
UI-LAW-001.statement: Users spend most of their time on other sites; interface layouts, navigation patterns, and iconography must conform to familiar mental models rather than inventing proprietary navigation mechanics.
UI-LAW-001.evidence_quote: Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.

UI-LAW-003.title: Hick's Law: Minimize Options to Reduce Decision Latency
UI-LAW-003.statement: Break down complex choices into distinct progressive steps; menus and selection dialogs should limit initial choices to high-frequency actions.
UI-LAW-003.evidence_quote: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices. Simplify choices for the user by breaking complex tasks into smaller steps.

UI-LAW-004.title: Miller's Law: Chunk Complex Information into 5 to 9 Discrete Units
UI-LAW-004.statement: Complex interfaces and forms must organize related information into discrete visual chunks containing no more than 7 (+/- 2) elements per group.
UI-LAW-004.evidence_quote: The average person can only keep 7 (plus or minus 2) items in their working memory. Organize content into smaller chunks to help users process and memorize easily.

UI-PER-001.title: Perceived Performance via Skeleton Loaders (Doherty Threshold)
UI-PER-001.statement: Content areas with predictable structure must render layout-matching Skeleton Shimmer loaders instead of spinning loaders during data retrieval.
UI-PER-001.evidence_quote: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other. Skeleton screens minimize perceived waiting time.

UI-STA-001.title: Mandatory Five-State Component Anatomy
UI-STA-001.statement: Every data-displaying component must explicitly implement all 5 UI states: Empty, Loading/Skeleton, Error (with retry), Success, and Interactive (Hover/Active/Disabled).
UI-STA-001.evidence_quote: Provide immediate feedback on system status and progress whenever an operation will take a noticeable amount of time to complete.
UI-STA-001.adaptation_note: Corrected 2026-09-13 audit: real Chapter 7 is "Lists of Things" and real Chapter 9 is "Showing Complex Data" — neither contains a "Progress Indicators and Responsive Feedback" section. The genuine matching content is the "Spinners and Loading Indicators" pattern in Chapter 8 (with a related pattern in Chapter 6). This rule's specific "5-state component anatomy" (Empty/Loading/Error-with-retry/Success/Interactive) formalism has no counterpart anywhere in this book — a search for "empty state," "five states," and "5 states" returns zero hits — and is retained as an independent, modern SaaS-engineering best practice beyond what this book documents.

inmemory-vs-distributed-lock.verdict: In-memory promise mutexes are STRICTLY CONFINED to single-process test doubles (Mock/Fake repositories). Production services MUST enforce concurrency at the Database layer (SELECT FOR UPDATE) or Distributed Lock layer (Redis Redlock).

incidents.symptom: High-load document upload caused Redis workers to crash with Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors.
incidents.root_cause: Workers ingested 50MB PDFs directly into memory as whole buffers rather than stream chunking.
incidents.knowledge_feedback: RAG-ING-002 (Streaming / Bounded-Buffer Parsing for Large Document Ingestion) was added 2026-09-15 to close this exact gap: it requires page-by-page/row-by-row incremental parsing with a hard memory cap, independent of the file-size dispatch threshold (RAG-ASY-001) or rate limiting (SEC-RAT-001). RAG-CHK-001 still only chunks text already resident in memory and remains structurally unable to prevent this failure by itself.

incidents.symptom: Concurrent wallet withdrawal requests allowed balance to drop below zero (lost update race condition).
incidents.root_cause: Service verified balance in-memory without row-level locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) before issuing update statement.
incidents.knowledge_feedback: frameworks/database-concurrency.framework.xml Branch 2 requires SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a short transaction for exactly this class of high-contention balance/inventory mutation. BE-DB-002 (prisma.$transaction wrapping for multi-table writes) alone does not prevent this incident: wrapping a read-then-write in a plain transaction does not stop two concurrent transactions from both reading the same pre-withdrawal balance and both committing their own deduction — that requires an explicit row lock (or an equivalent optimistic-concurrency version check), which is what FW-CON-001 Branch 2 actually specifies.
